paper.title: Distinct cerebrospinal fluid microbiome dysbiosis associated with disease severity in tick-borne encephalitis
paper.authors: Chaopreecha J, Suyema S, Fořtová A, Pychova M, Krbkova L, Blair GE, Sheppard SK, Ruzek D, Goonawardane N.

steps.evidence: Base-calling of 16S rRNA sequencing was run by the Dorado (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, v.0.6.1).
Sequencing reads that passed the filtering conditions (mean Q score > 8) were analysed by EPI2ME (Oxford Nanopore Technologies) for bacterial classification.
Sequencing reads that passed the filtering conditions (mean Q score > 8) were analysed by EPI2ME (Oxford Nanopore Technologies) for bacterial classification.

Negative (buffer) controls processed alongside CSF samples were used to identify taxa enriched in controls, which were classified as high-confidence contaminants and removed prior to downstream analyses
with additional prevalence- and biology-informed filtering applied to taxa shared between CSF and controls and removal of non-bacterial 16S artifacts
Alpha diversity was assessed at the species level using the Shannon diversity index and Simpson diversity index. In addition, species richness was estimated using the Chao1 index.
Beta diversity was evaluated using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity calculated from species-level relative abundance data.
Differentially abundant taxa across groups were identified using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.
Associations between selected taxa and clinical groups were assessed using Kruskal-Wallis tests or Spearman correlation, as appropriate, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.

For machine learning analysis, a random forest classifier was trained on species-level relative abundance data to evaluate the ability of microbial profiles to discriminate between clinical groups (encephalitis and meningitis).
Taxonomic composition was visualized using stacked bar plots at the phylum, genus, and species levels, displaying the 12 most abundant taxa per group.

paper.authors: Carta G, Xian F, Malzl D, Schmidt M, David Gómez-Varela1.

steps.evidence: The protein preparation protocol as previously described[], started by taking 30–50 mg of FS that was mixed with 200 μL of lysis buffer (5% SDS, 2 M urea, 50 mM Tris-HCl, protease inhibitor 1x) and vortexed vigorously for 1 min.
The samples were then placed in a Thermomixer (serial number: 5382JR638726, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany), at 1,200 rpm and 70°C for 15 min.
The samples were then ultrasonicated using a Bioruptor Pico (Diagenode, SeraMTAB, Belgium, program: 15 cycles of 30 s “on” and 30 s “off”, frequency level: Low, water temperature: +20°C).
At room temperature, the tubes were then centrifuged for 5 minutes at 16,000 g.
A modified version of the one-pot solid-phase enhanced sample preparation method (SP3) of Hughes et al.[] is used for protein purification and digestion was used.
Samples went through the processes of protein reduction (5 mM dithiothreitol, DTT, incubated for 30 min at + 60°C) and alkylation (20 mM iodoacetamide, IAA, 30 min in the dark at room temperature).
The remaining IAA in the sample was quenched by adding DTT at a final concentration of 5 mM.
Premixed Sera-Mag SpeedBead beads were added in a volume of 10 μL (50 mg/mL, Cytiva, Marlborough, MA) to a 50 μg protein sample.
One volume of absolute ethanol was immediately added to initiate the protein binding to the beads, followed by incubation and agitation at 1,000 rpm for 5 min at 24°C in a Thermomixer.
After standing on a magnetic rack for 2 minutes, the supernatant was removed, and the beads were rinsed three times with 500 μL of 80% ethanol.
The obtained beads were reconstituted in 50 μL of digestion buffer (50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8).
2 μg of sequencing grade trypsin/LysC (Promega, Madison, USA) was used for protein digestion in a Thermomimixer with agitation at 950 rpm for 18 h at 37°C.
After a 30-second spin, acetonitrile (ACN) was added to each sample to reach a final concentration of 95%.
The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 8 minutes and then placed on a magnetic rack for 2 minutes.
After the supernatant was discarded 900μL of 100% ACN was added, 15 seconds on a magnetic rack and removed from each tube.
To elute the peptides, the washed beads were reconstituted in 20 μL of liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) grade water.
Peptide concentrations were measured in duplicate at 205 nm using a NanoPhotontometer N60 (serial number: TG2022, Implen, Munich, Germany).
A final concentration of 0.1% Formic acid (FA) was added to acidify peptides and the tubes were stored at − 20°C until LC-MS/MS analysis.
The built-in taxonomy and function databases were created by importing into iMeta\text{MetaLab} (v2.3.0)
peptide and protein tables were generated with MaxLFQ[]
Tables with peptide and intensities data (microbial and host) were adopted for taxonomical annotation (Ignore blanks under rank: Unique peptide count ≥ 3, Superkingdom)
The taxonomy annotation output from iMetalab was further processed in R by removing peptides without taxonomic annotations and taxa annotated by fewer than three distinct peptides
Alpha and Beta diversity indexes, engraftment analyses, and taxa-function were calculated at the Species level.
From the iMetaLab function annotation table, the KEGG pathways identified by fewer than 3 proteins were removed
To define the Species-specific functions Meta4P[] was used
Meta4P results were filtered by the Species-NOG pathway identified by at least 3 peptides.
We performed consensus clustering on KEGG pathway z-score profiles.

Consensus clustering was then performed for k values ranging from 2 to 6, using the following parameters: 500 bootstrap resampling iterations, with each iteration subsampling 80% of the samples and 80% of the features without replacement.
Considering the factors time, cohort, and sex of the pups, and their interactions when detecting a significant difference with the Kruskal-Wallis test with BH correction
a soft clustering (allowing proteins to belong to multiple clusters) with the Mfuzz R package was performed[]

Proteins with the highest membership were searched for Multiple Proteins by Names / Identifiers on String 12.0 (https://stringdb.org; 23/05/2025) and protein full STRING networks were obtained with confidence as a parameter for meaning of the network edges, with a minimum required interaction score of 0.7.
The food protein dataset was generated using the FASTA file created by Valdes and colleagues [] through FragPipe (https://fragfile.nesvilab.org/) to generate a reduced protein list.

Genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 and a |fold2change| ≥ 1, were considered differentially expressed
